q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'impact' of a tax from its 'incidence'?

options.A: The impact of a tax is the final burden borne by the person who ultimately pays it, while its incidence is the first point at which it is collected
options.B: The impact and the incidence of a tax are two names for one and the same burden, falling always on the same person
options.C: The impact of a tax is its first point of contact with the taxpayer, while its incidence is the point of its final resting place after shifting
options.D: The impact of a tax can never be shifted to another person, while its incidence is shifted in every case

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the ability-to-pay approach to taxation from the benefit approach?

options.A: Under the ability-to-pay approach, a person is taxed in proportion to the benefits he receives from public expenditure
options.B: Under the benefit approach, a person is taxed strictly according to his income and wealth, irrespective of the benefits received
options.C: The two approaches are identical, both requiring the tax burden to be distributed in proportion to income
options.D: Under the ability-to-pay approach, a person is taxed according to his capacity to pay, while under the benefit approach he is taxed in proportion to the benefits received by him from public expenditure

options.C: The same rate of tax is applied to all taxpayers, irrespective of the size of the tax base
options.D: The amount of tax payable remains the same for every taxpayer, irrespective of the tax base

q: 'Pump priming' in public finance refers to:

options.B: Financing of the fiscal deficit of the Government through market borrowings and treasury bills
options.C: A relatively small, one-time injection of Government spending intended to revive private investment and set the economy moving again
options.D: An increase in taxation by the Government intended to withdraw purchasing power and curb inflation

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four canons of taxation enunciated by Adam Smith?
The canon of certainty in taxation requires that:

options.A: The tax payable by a person, and the time and manner of its payment, should be clear, plain and certain, and not arbitrary
options.B: The tax should be collected at the time and in the manner most convenient to the contributor
options.C: The cost of collecting the tax should be as small as possible in proportion to its yield
options.D: Every person should contribute to the revenue of the State in proportion to his ability to pay

q: The 'displacement effect' in the growth of public expenditure, associated with Peacock and Wiseman, refers to:

options.B: A step-like increase in public expenditure during a social disturbance, such as a war, after which the expenditure does not return to its earlier lower level
options.C: The displacement of tax revenue from the States to the Centre following a tax reform
options.D: The transfer of expenditure from the revenue account to the capital account of the Government

q: The Planning, Programming and Budgeting System (PPBS) is primarily characterised by:

options.B: Providing in each year's budget only a small incremental addition over the expenditure of the previous year
options.C: Linking expenditure to programmes and objectives, with an analysis of the costs and benefits of alternative ways of achieving them over a multi-year horizon
options.D: Justifying every programme and item of expenditure afresh from a zero base in each year's budget

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a specific tax from an ad valorem tax?

options.A: A specific tax is levied as a percentage of the value of the commodity, while an ad valorem tax is levied per unit of its weight or quantity
options.B: A specific tax is levied only on imports, while an ad valorem tax is levied only on domestic production
options.C: A specific tax is levied per unit of the weight, quantity or measurement of the commodity, while an ad valorem tax is levied as a percentage of its value
options.D: A specific tax can be shifted to another person, while an ad valorem tax can never be shifted

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes tax evasion from tax avoidance?

options.A: Tax evasion is a lawful arrangement for reducing tax liability, while tax avoidance is an offence punishable under the tax laws
options.B: Tax evasion and tax avoidance are two names for the same practice, both being offences under the tax laws
options.C: Tax avoidance consists of concealing income and falsifying accounts, while tax evasion consists of arranging transactions within the framework of the law
options.D: Tax evasion is the illegal non-payment of tax by concealing income or falsifying records, while tax avoidance is the lawful arrangement of transactions so as to reduce tax liability within the framework of the law

q: A tax is described as 'degressive' when:

options.A: The rate of tax rises with the size of the tax base, but less than proportionately, so that the progression becomes milder at the higher levels of the base
options.B: The rate of tax falls continuously as the tax base increases, at all levels of the base
options.C: The same fixed amount of tax is payable by every taxpayer, irrespective of the size of the tax base
options.D: The rate of tax rises more than proportionately at every level of increase in the tax base

q: A tax is described as 'regressive' when:

options.A: The rate of tax increases as the tax base, such as income, increases
options.B: The rate of tax decreases as the tax base increases, so that the tax takes a smaller proportion of a larger tax base
options.C: The same rate of tax is applied to all taxpayers, irrespective of the size of the tax base
options.D: The amount of tax is fixed per unit of the commodity taxed, irrespective of its value

q: In the Peacock-Wiseman analysis of the growth of public expenditure, the 'inspection effect' refers to:

options.A: The tendency of public expenditure to rise in steps during a war or other social disturbance and not to return to its earlier level afterwards
options.B: The concentration of public expenditure in the hands of the Central Government in a federal set-up
options.C: The revelation, during a period of disturbance and closer scrutiny of public affairs, of neglected problems and inadequacies in existing services, leading to new demands for public expenditure
options.D: The inspection of Government expenditure by the audit authorities before it is incurred

q: In the Peacock-Wiseman analysis of the growth of public expenditure, the 'concentration effect' refers to:

options.A: The concentration of the tax burden on a small number of large taxpayers
options.B: The tendency of expenditure to be concentrated in the closing months of the financial year
options.C: The concentration of audit objections on a small number of spending departments
options.D: The tendency, in a federal system, for the Central Government to grow faster than the State and local governments, so that public activity becomes increasingly concentrated at the Centre

q: The doctrine of 'functional finance', associated with Abba P. Lerner, holds that:

options.B: Public borrowing should be resorted to only for financing capital works that yield a direct monetary return
options.C: Fiscal measures should be judged by their effects on the economy, such as employment and price stability, and the budget should be used to maintain aggregate demand at the level needed for full employment, rather than being balanced as an end in itself
options.D: The functions of taxation and public expenditure should be divided between the Centre and the States strictly in proportion to their revenues
